rows.evidence: Q1: Materials and Methods, Field Experiments <U+2014> a two-season (2017, 2018) field experiment on a calcareous sandy soil at Sohag, Egypt, split-plot design with four replications, testing three P fertigation frequencies and two P forms; own yield, petiole P, soil pH/available P, PUE and WUE data reported in Tables 4-6 and Figs. 1-2.
rows.notes: The study has no own result on drip irrigation as the technology producing the claimed effect. All plots were drip-irrigated with the same daily water amount; the only factors varied were P fertigation frequency (daily, every 2 or 3 days) and P form (urea phosphate vs monopotassium phosphate). It does not compare drip with other irrigation methods, does not measure water distribution uniformity, waterlogging, dry patches or plant stress, and does not attribute yield to the irrigation method. What it shows is that daily fertigation with urea phosphate lowered soil pH, raised available P and petiole P, and increased marketable yield (about 10% for daily vs less frequent application; 22% for daily UP vs MPP every 3 days) and PUE/WUE on this sandy calcareous soil. The passage's statements about uniform water distribution and reduced stress/yield-reduction risk from drip are not tested here; the study's framing of drip benefits (Introduction, Conclusions) rests on cited literature and general assertion.

rows.evidence: Q1: Materials and Methods <U+2014> own two-season field experiment (2017, 2018) on calcareous sandy soil in Sohag, Egypt, split-plot with four replications, measuring soil pH, available P, petiole P, tuber yield, PUE, WUE and IWUE under P fertigation treatments (Tables 4-6, Figs. 1-2).
rows.notes: No own evidence on drip irrigation reducing the risk of plant stress or yield reduction, or preventing waterlogging/dry patches. Drip was the uniform background irrigation system for every treatment (same daily water, 30-40 m3/ha, based on Penman-Monteith ETc); no alternative irrigation method, no measurement of water distribution uniformity, soil moisture variability, plant stress or risk/variability of yield. The study's own findings concern P fertigation frequency and P form: daily urea phosphate fertigation lowered soil pH by about 7%, raised available P by about 24% vs MPP, raised petiole P and gave the highest yields, PUE and WUE. Risk reduction attributable to drip is asserted in the Introduction/Conclusions from cited work only.

notes: Full text appears complete (abstract through references). The study is a primary field trial of P fertigation management under drip irrigation; drip itself was not a treatment variable, so the review's attribution of uniform water distribution and reduced stress risk to drip is not supported by this study's own results.
